real text layer; questions and memo answers were extracted with pdftotext
(-layout) and read page by page against the official Marking Guidelines.
The memo is bilingual (English/Afrikaans); only the ENGLISH content is
transcribed here. Every question and sub-question is transcribed at full
fidelity; diagrams, graphs and experimental setups are described in
bracketed words. solution_method is the method the MEMO uses - the
matcher's content signal. Decimal commas are kept as printed (SA convention).

questions.text: Multiple choice: Several forces are acting on a moving object. Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT when these forces are in equilibrium? A The velocity of the object is increasing. B The object is moving at a constant velocity. C The kinetic energy of the object is decreasing. D The object has a non-zero acceleration.

Multiple choice: A stone thrown vertically downwards from the top of a building takes t seconds to strike the ground. Consider the acceleration-time graph for the motion of the stone. The effects of air friction are ignored. [Graph: acceleration (m·s⁻²) constant at 9,8 from 0 to t seconds; the area under the graph between 0 and t is shaded.] What does the shaded area between 0 and t seconds, shown in the graph, represent? A The final velocity of the stone B The change in position of the stone C The constant velocity of the stone D The change in velocity of the stone

Multiple choice: A ball moving horizontally has constant momentum p and kinetic energy K. The ball collides with a wall and bounces back horizontally. Immediately after the collision, the ball has momentum ½p. The mass of the ball remains constant. [Diagram: ball moving with momentum p towards a wall; after bouncing it moves away with momentum ½p.] Which ONE of the following is the kinetic energy of the ball immediately after the collision? A ¼K B ½K C 2K D 4K

Multiple choice: A force F acts on a box as the box moves from rest down a rough incline at a constant acceleration. The force is parallel to the incline, as shown in the diagram. [Diagram: box on an incline with force F directed up the slope, box moving down the slope.] Choose the option that CORRECTLY completes the following statement: The work done by the gravitational force is ... the work done by the frictional force and the work done by F. A equal to the sum of B less than the sum of C greater than the sum of D equal to the difference between

Multiple choice: A ball falling vertically downwards from point A strikes the ground with velocity v and bounces, reaching a maximum height at point B, as shown in the diagram. [Diagram: point A above point B; B is the lower maximum-rebound height above the ground.] Which ONE of the combinations below is CORRECT for the direction of the impulse on the ball upon striking the ground and the magnitude of the velocity with which the ball leaves the ground? A Upward; Greater than v B Downward; Greater than v C Upward; Less than v D Downward; Less than v

Multiple choice: The absorption spectrum of an element surrounding a moving star is observed on Earth and found to be red shifted. Which ONE of the following combinations is CORRECT for the movement of the star and the frequency of the observed light on Earth? A Away from Earth; Decreased B Towards Earth; Decreased C Away from Earth; Increased D Towards Earth; Increased

Multiple choice: Two small identical spheres, each with mass m and charge +Q, are placed in a vertical cylinder. The spheres remain stationary when their centres are r metres apart, as shown in the diagram. Ignore ALL frictional effects. [Diagram: vertical cylinder with one charged sphere (+Q, mass m) floating a distance r above an identical sphere (+Q, mass m) at the bottom.] Which ONE of the following expressions can be used to CORRECTLY calculate the distance r? A √(kQ²/mg) B √(kmg/Q²) C √(Q²/kmg) D √(mg/kQ²)
Multiple choice: The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of ... A power. B electric current. C electrical energy. D potential difference.

Multiple choice: The diagram shows a simplified electric motor. The rotation of the coil is observed from the battery. [Diagram: rectangular coil between magnetic poles N (left) and S (right), connected via a split-ring commutator to a battery.] Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT while the motor is in operation? The coil and the ... A slip rings rotate anti-clockwise. B slip rings rotate clockwise. C commutator rotate clockwise. D commutator rotate anti-clockwise.

Multiple choice: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for the photoelectric effect? The photoelectric effect demonstrates that: (i) Light has a wave nature (ii) Light has a particle nature (iii) Light energy is quantised. A (i) only B (ii) only C (i) and (iii) only D (ii) and (iii) only

questions.text: In an experiment, a crate of mass 8,5 kg, lying stationary on a rough horizontal table, is connected to a mass hanger by means of a light inextensible string passing over a frictionless pulley. Mass pieces are added to the mass hanger and the acceleration of the crate is measured. The experiment is repeated several times by adding different masses to increase the hanging mass each time. Ignore the effects of air friction. [Diagram: 8,5 kg crate on a horizontal table, string over a pulley at the table edge down to a mass hanger with mass pieces.] The results obtained were used to draw a sketch graph of acceleration of crate (m·s⁻²) versus hanging mass (kg): [Graph: acceleration remains zero up to a hanging mass of 4,2 kg, then increases; the acceleration at hanging mass 7,4 kg is labelled Y.] 2.1 Define the term static friction.
questions.memo_answer: The force that opposes the tendency of motion of a stationary object relative/parallel to a surface.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing ALL the HORIZONTAL forces acting on the crate JUST BEFORE it starts moving.
questions.memo_answer: [Free-body diagram: dot with static friction fs to the left and tension T to the right (directions may be mirrored).] Accepted labels: fs = static friction/f/Ff; T = FT/Fstring/tension. Do not penalise if vertical forces (w, N) are shown; mark awarded for label and arrow; if arrows do not touch the dot max 1/2; any additional force except w and N max 1/2; correct but no arrows max 1/2.

questions.text: Calculate the coefficient of static friction (µs). [From the graph the crate starts to move when the hanging mass is 4,2 kg.]
questions.memo_working: OPTION 1: For hanging mass: Fnet = ma; mg – T = 0, so T = mg = 4,2(9,8) = 41,16 N. For crate: fs(max) = T; µsN = T; µs(8,5)(9,8) = 41,16; µs = 0,49. OPTION 2: fs(max) = T = w(hanging); µsN = m(hanging)g; µs(8,5)(9,8) = 4,2(9,8) OR µs(8,5) = 4,2; µs = 0,49.

questions.text: Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration represented by Y on the graph if the coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the table is 0,40. [Y is the acceleration at a hanging mass of 7,4 kg.]
questions.memo_working: For crate: Fnet = ma; T – fk = ma; T – 0,4(8,5)(9,8) = 8,5a ... Eqn (1). For hanging mass: Fnet = ma; mg – T = ma; 7,4(9,8) – T = 7,4a ... Eqn (2). Solving: Y = a = 2,47 (m·s⁻²). NOTE: T can be calculated first (54,32 N).

questions.text: A 5 kg block is now placed inside the crate and the experiment is repeated. How will this affect the maximum static frictional force now experienced by the crate? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME. Give a reason for the answer.
questions.memo_answer: INCREASES. fs(max) ∝ N OR fs(max) ∝ m OR fs(max) = µsN OR the normal force acting on the crate increases OR increase in mass/weight of crate (increases the normal force).

questions.text: Ball A is thrown vertically upwards at 12 m·s⁻¹ from the top of a building. Two seconds after ball A was thrown upwards, ball B is thrown vertically downwards at 5,4 m·s⁻¹ from the top of the same building. Both balls, A and B, strike the ground at time t seconds. Ignore the effects of air friction. [Graph: position-time sketch graphs for both balls; ball A rises from the top of the building (position Z above the ground) to a maximum position Y, then falls to the ground at time t; ball B starts at Z at 2 s and moves down to the ground, also reaching it at time t.] Using EQUATIONS OF MOTION ONLY, calculate the value of t as shown in the graphs.
questions.memo_working: Taking upwards as positive: Ball A: Δy = viΔt + ½aΔt² = 12t + ½(–9,8)t² ... Eqn (1). Ball B: Δy = –5,4(t – 2) + ½(–9,8)(t – 2)² ... Eqn (2). Setting 12t + ½(–9,8)t² = –5,4(t – 2) + ½(–9,8)(t – 2)² gives t = 4 (s). (Memo also gives the downwards-as-positive equivalent and options substituting x = t – 2 for ball B or splitting ball A's motion at its turning point, t = 2,45 s.)

questions.text: Using EQUATIONS OF MOTION ONLY, calculate the value of Z, as shown in the graphs. [Z is the starting position of the balls, i.e. the height of the top of the building above the ground.]
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 3.1.1. Upwards positive, OPTION 1 (Ball A): Δy = viΔt + ½aΔt² = (12)(4) + ½(–9,8)(4)² = –30,4 m, so Z = 30,4 (m). OPTION 2 (Ball B): Δy = (–5,4)(4 – 2) + ½(–9,8)(4 – 2)² = –30,4 m, so Z = 30,4 (m). (Memo also gives options using vf² = vi² + 2aΔy with vf = –27,2 m·s⁻¹ or –25 m·s⁻¹, and Δy = ((vi + vf)/2)Δt.)

questions.text: Using EQUATIONS OF MOTION ONLY, calculate the value of Y, as shown in the graphs. [Y is the maximum position reached by ball A above the ground.]
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 3.1.1 and 3.1.2. Ball A: vf² = vi² + 2aΔy; 0 = (12)² + 2(–9,8)Δy; Δy = 7,35 m. Then Y = 7,35 + 30,4 = 37,75 (m). (Memo options also allow finding Δt = 1,22 s from vf = vi + aΔt then Δy = ((vi + vf)/2)Δt = 7,32 m, or Δy = viΔt + ½aΔt² = 7,35 m.)

questions.text: On the same set of axes, sketch the velocity-time graphs for ball A and ball B while they are in free fall. Label the graphs A and B for ball A and ball B respectively. Clearly indicate the following on the graphs: the initial velocity of each ball; the time at which each ball is thrown; the time at which the balls strike the ground.
questions.memo_answer: [Sketch (upwards positive): straight line A starting at +12 m·s⁻¹ at t = 0 with constant negative slope, crossing zero at 2 s (turning point implied) and ending at 4 s; straight line B starting at –5,4 m·s⁻¹ at t = 2 s, parallel to A and to the right of A, ending at 4 s. Downwards-positive mirror image also accepted.] Marking criteria: correct initial velocities with correct shape (straight lines, both positive or both negative slopes); correct starting times with B starting after the time-axis intercept of A; both graphs end at 4 s (accept t); graphs parallel with B to the right of A. NB: no labels A and B, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Two trolleys, A and B, of masses of 1,5 kg and 2 kg respectively, are held in a stationary position on a straight, horizontal, frictionless track, with a compressed spring between them. The trolleys are released and the spring takes t seconds to return to its natural length. The spring then falls to the ground. Trolley A moves to the left, while trolley B moves to the right and then up a frictionless inclined plane, rising to a maximum vertical height of 1,5 m. [Diagram: before release, trolleys A (1,5 kg) and B (2 kg) with compressed spring between them; after release, A moves left, B moves right and rises 1,5 m up an incline.] Ignore the rotational effects of the wheels. 4.1 Write down the principle of conservation of mechanical energy in words.
questions.memo_answer: The total mechanical energy / sum of gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, in an isolated system remains constant / is conserved.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Calculate the speed of trolley B at the bottom of the inclined plane.
questions.memo_working: OPTION 1: (Ep + Ek)top = (Ep + Ek)bottom; (2)(9,8)(1,5) + 0 = 0 + ½(2)v²; v = 5,42 m·s⁻¹. OPTION 2: Wnc = ΔEk + ΔEp; 0 = [0 – ½vi²] + [(9,8)(1,5 – 0)]; vi = 5,42 m·s⁻¹. (Memo also gives Wnet = ΔEk with FgΔycos180°, ΔEk = –ΔEp, and vf² = vi² + 2aΔx options.)

questions.text: For the t seconds that the spring takes to return to its natural length: Calculate the change in momentum of trolley B.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 4.2. Δp = mvf – mvi = 2(5,42 – 0) = 10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ right (OR 2(–5,42 – 0) = –10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹).

questions.text: For the t seconds that the spring takes to return to its natural length: Write down the change in momentum of trolley A.
questions.memo_answer: 10,84 kg·m·s⁻¹ left / opposite direction. (POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 4.3.1.)

questions.text: Calculate the speed of trolley A after t seconds.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 4.2 and 4.3.1. ΔpA = mvf – mvi: –10,84 = 1,5(vf – 0); vf = –7,23 m·s⁻¹, so v = 7,23 m·s⁻¹. OR Σpi = Σpf: 0 = 1,5vf + (2)(5,42); vf = –7,23 m·s⁻¹; v = 7,23 m·s⁻¹.

questions.text: A constant force F is applied at an angle of 30° to the horizontal on a crate of mass 6 kg that is initially at rest. A constant frictional force of 10 N acts on the crate as it moves from rest at point A along a horizontal surface to point B. The distance between point A and point B is 1,5 m. The speed of the crate at point B is 2 m·s⁻¹. [Diagram: 6 kg crate on a horizontal surface pulled by force F at 30° above the horizontal over the 1,5 m from A to B.] 5.1 Define the term work done by a force.
questions.memo_answer: The work done on an object by a constant force F is FΔxcosθ, where F is the magnitude of the force, Δx the magnitude of the displacement and θ the angle between the force and the displacement. OR The work done on an object is the product of the force and the displacement of the object in the direction of the displacement.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing ALL the forces acting on the crate as it moves.
questions.memo_answer: [Free-body diagram: dot with normal force N upward, weight w downward, applied force F at 30° above the horizontal (to the right), friction f horizontally opposite to the motion (to the left). Mirror image accepted.] Accepted labels: w = Fw/Fg/mg/58,8 N/gravitational force/weight; f = Ff/fk/(kinetic) friction; N = FN/normal force; F = FA/applied force. Notes: mark awarded for label and arrow; additional forces max 3/4; no arrows max 3/4; forces not touching the dot max 3/4; components drawn for F max 3/4.

questions.text: Using ENERGY PRINCIPLES ONLY, calculate the magnitude of force F.
questions.memo_note: The memo marking-criteria block states 'Correct final answer: 20,79 N' while all worked options give 20,78 N; the accepted range 20,769 – 20,79 N covers both.

questions.text: A 2 kg object is placed in the crate. What effect will this have on the work done by the same force F when the crate is again moved from point A to point B? Write only INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME.

A stationary listener, standing on the roadside, records the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren of a police car travelling at a constant velocity. In the wavelength-time graph, NOT drawn to scale, λL is the wavelength of the sound recorded by the listener and λS is the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren. Take the speed of sound in air to be 343 m·s⁻¹. [Graph: two horizontal lines of wavelength versus time; λL = 0,40 m (upper line) and λS = 0,38 m (lower line).] 6.1 Name the phenomenon that explains why the wavelengths shown in the graph differ.
Is the car moving TOWARDS or AWAY FROM the listener? Give a reason for the answer.
questions.memo_answer: Away from. Wavelength of sound detected/observed by the listener is longer than wavelength of sound emitted by the source OR frequency detected by the listener is lower than the frequency of the source OR λL > λS OR fL < fS.

questions.text: Calculate the frequency of the sound emitted by the siren.
questions.memo_working: v = fλ; 343 = f(0,38); f = 902,63 Hz. (If c = fλ used, penalise 1 mark; if 340 used, penalise 1 mark for answer.)

questions.text: Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the car.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 6.3.1. v = fλ; 343 = f(0,4); fL = 857,5 Hz. Then fL = v/(v + vs) × fS: 857,5 = (343/(343 + vs))(902,63); vs = 18,05 m·s⁻¹. (If wavelengths are substituted instead of frequencies max 2/6; if wavelengths are swopped max 3/6.)

questions.text: P is a +2 nC point charge. X is a point 6 cm away from charge P. [Diagram: charge P (+2 nC) with point X 6 cm to its right.] Calculate the magnitude of the electric field at X.
Point charge S, with a charge of −2 nC, is placed 4 cm to the right of charge P. [Diagram: P (+2 nC) and S (−2 nC) 4 cm apart.] Draw the resultant electric field pattern due to charges P and S.
questions.memo_answer: [Sketch: field pattern of two unlike charges - field lines leaving the positive charge P and entering the negative charge S, curving between them, plus outer lines.] Criteria: correct direction of field lines; correct shape of the electric field lines between charges and on the outside of the charges; no field lines crossing each other, field lines must touch the charge but not go inside the charge. Note: field pattern of two like charges 0/3; only one charge drawn 0/3.

questions.text: A third point charge T is placed 2 cm to the right of S. Point charge T experiences a net electrostatic force of 2,5 x 10⁻⁴ N to the left. [Diagram: P (+2 nC), S (−2 nC) 4 cm to the right of P, and T 2 cm to the right of S.] State Coulomb's law in words.
questions.memo_answer: The magnitude of the electrostatic force exerted by one point charge on another point charge is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any underlined key words/phrases omitted, deduct 1 mark; if reference to masses or the word FORCE in context omitted, 0/2.

questions.text: What is the polarity of charge T? Choose from POSITIVE or NEGATIVE.
Calculate the magnitude of charge T.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM Q7.1 IN TERMS OF CONVERSIONS. OPTION 1: F = kQ1Q2/r² for both: FST = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)QT/(0,02)² and FPT = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)QT/(0,06)². Fnet = FST – FPT: 2,5 x 10⁻⁴ = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)QT/(0,02)² − (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)QT/(0,06)²; QT = 6,25 x 10⁻⁹ C. OPTION 2: ES = (9 x 10⁹)(2 x 10⁻⁹)/0,02² = 45 000 N·C⁻¹; Enet = EP – ES = 5 x 10³ − 45 000 = –4 x 10⁴ N·C⁻¹; F = Eq: –2,5 x 10⁻⁴ = (–4 x 10⁴)QT; QT = 6,25 x 10⁻⁹ C.

questions.text: L1 and L2 are two light bulbs that have the following ratings: L1: 36 W ; 20 V and L2: 48 W ; 32 V. The two bulbs are connected as shown in the circuit diagram. The battery has an internal resistance of 0,6 Ω while the conducting wires and the ammeters have negligible resistance. R1 and R2 are resistors. [Circuit diagram: battery with emf ε and internal resistance r = 0,6 Ω; ammeter A1 in the main circuit; resistor R2 = 4 Ω in series with the parallel section; the parallel section has two branches: branch 1 contains ammeter A2 and bulb L2, branch 2 contains resistor R1 in series with bulb L1.] 8.1 Define the term power.
questions.memo_answer: The rate at which work is done/dissipated OR energy transferred OR work done per unit time. (2 or 0)

questions.text: If both light bulbs operate as RATED, calculate the reading on ammeter A2.
questions.memo_working: OPTION 1: P = VI; 48 = 32I; I = 1,5 A. OPTION 2: P = V²/R; 48 = 32²/R; R = 21,33 Ω; then P = I²R or V = IR gives I = 1,5 A.

questions.text: If both light bulbs operate as RATED, calculate the reading on ammeter A1.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 8.2.1. For L1: P = VI; 36 = 20I; I = 1,8 A (or via R = 20²/36 = 11,11 Ω). ITOT = 1,5 + 1,8 = 3,3 A.

questions.text: If both light bulbs operate as RATED, calculate the resistance of resistor R1.
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 8.2.2. OPTION 1: VR1 + VL1 = V(parallel); VR1 + 20 = 32; VR1 = 12 V; V = IR; 12 = 1,8R1; R1 = 6,67 Ω. OPTION 2: 32 = 1,8R; R = 17,77 Ω; RL1 = 20²/36 = 11,11 Ω; R1 = 17,77 – 11,11 = 6,67 Ω.

questions.text: If both light bulbs operate as RATED, calculate the emf of the battery.

Bulb L1 burns out after a while. Assume that the resistance of bulb L2 remains constant. Will bulb L2 continue to glow after bulb L1 burns out? Choose from YES or NO. Support your answer with a suitable calculation.
questions.memo_answer: NO (accept: not glow). RL2 = 32²/48 = 21,33 Ω (or 32/1,5); ε = I(R + r): 47,18 = I(21,33 + 4 + 0,6); I = 1,82 A. [The current through L2 exceeds its rated current of 1,5 A, so L2 burns out.]
questions.memo_working: POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 8.2.1 and 8.2.4. If 21,33 Ω already calculated previously, award mark.

questions.text: The graph shows how the induced current in a generator varies with time. [Graph: induced current (A) versus time (s); the current rises from 0 to a peak of 1,2 A and returns to 0 at 0,02 s, repeating identical positive humps between 0,02–0,04 s (current never goes negative); gridlines at 0,01, 0,02, 0,03, 0,04 s.] Name the type of generator. Choose from AC or DC.
State the energy conversion that takes place in this generator while it is in operation.
Give a reason why this generator is NOT suitable for the transmission of electricity over long distances.
questions.memo_answer: Power/energy/voltage loss cannot be reduced / will be too large OR I (current) cannot be made smaller. Accept: transformers do not use DC / cannot be stepped up or down.

questions.text: Calculate the frequency at which the coil rotates in the generator.
questions.memo_working: f = 1/T = 1/0,02 = 50 Hz OR f = number of waves/time = 2/0,04 = 50 Hz.

questions.text: Define the term root mean square (rms) current.
questions.memo_answer: Root-mean-square current is the alternating current that dissipates the same amount of energy as an equivalent DC current.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Calculate the root-mean-square current delivered by the generator.

The graph shows how the induced current varies with time after a change was made to the operation of the generator. [Graph: same shape as before but the peak current is now 0,6 A and one full hump takes 0,04 s (double the original period).] Fully describe the change that was made.
questions.memo_answer: Speed of rotation halved. Accept: frequency was halved / period was doubled. If only 'speed of rotation slower / frequency decreases / period increased': 1/2.

questions.text: Define the term photoelectric effect.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_answer: The process whereby electrons are ejected from a metal surface when light (of suitable frequency) is incident/shining on that surface.
questions.memo_note: Memo instruction: if any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.

questions.text: Red light, blue light and green light are shone simultaneously on a sheet of potassium. Each colour of light consists of a single frequency. Two maximum kinetic energies of the ejected electrons are possible, namely 6,96 x 10⁻²⁰ J and 2,65 x 10⁻²⁰ J. Each ejected electron has only one of these maximum kinetic energies. [Diagram: red, blue and green light incident on a potassium sheet.] Which colour of light is responsible for ejecting electrons that have a maximum kinetic energy equal to 2,65 x 10⁻²⁰ J?
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials

questions.text: Explain the answer to QUESTION 10.2.1.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_answer: Only green and blue light eject electrons / red light does not eject electrons. Green has a lower frequency than blue / green has longer wavelength than blue / photons of blue light have more energy than photons of green light, and therefore [green] ejects electrons with the lower kinetic energy. (fgreen < fblue / blue has a higher frequency than green.)

questions.text: The electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 2,65 x 10⁻²⁰ J are ejected by light that has a frequency of 5,85 x 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the frequency of the light that ejected electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 6,96 x 10⁻²⁰ J.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_working: OPTION 1: E = W0 + Ek(max); hf = W0 + Ek(max); (6,63 x 10⁻³⁴)(5,85 x 10¹⁴) = W0 + 2,65 x 10⁻²⁰; W0 = 3,61 x 10⁻¹⁹ J. Then hf = W0 + Ek(max): (6,63 x 10⁻³⁴)f = 3,61 x 10⁻¹⁹ + 6,96 x 10⁻²⁰; f = 6,5 x 10¹⁴ Hz. OPTION 2: hf1 − Ek(max)1 = hf2 − Ek(max)2. OPTION 3: via threshold frequency f0 = 5,45 x 10¹⁴ Hz.

questions.text: The intensity of the red light is increased, while the intensities of the blue light and green light remain the same. What effect will this change have on the rate at which electrons are ejected? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials

questions.text: Some of the atoms of a hot gas, made up of a single element, are in an excited state. The spectrum formed by the hot gas is observed on a screen in a darkened room. The spectrum consists of specific coloured lines on a black background. Name the type of spectrum formed.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials

questions.text: Explain the presence of the coloured lines in the spectrum.
questions.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials
questions.memo_answer: Coloured lines represent (associated) frequencies/wavelengths/energy of the emitted (photons) when atoms/electrons move to a lower energy level.
